name: CrossOver
tagline: Runs Windows apps and games on macOS and Linux without a Windows license or a virtual machine.

pricing.notes: AI-drafted from a site submission; price unverified.

verdictSummary: CrossOver is a commercial packaging of Wine, and yes, Wine is free, which is exactly why this looks easier than it is. You can install Wine yourself today with a package manager and get a large fraction of the value in an afternoon, but that is not a build, that is using the upstream project. What CrossOver actually sells is the part nobody one-shots: thousands of per-application patches, DXVK and driver plumbing tuned per title, macOS specifics like the 32-bit and Rosetta mess, and a tested bottle configuration for each app so you do not spend a weekend bisecting registry keys. An agent can write you a slick GUI over Wine prefixes in one sitting. It cannot write the compatibility knowledge that makes a specific version of Office or a specific anti-cheat game actually launch.
coreLoopDIY: A local GUI that creates, lists and launches named Wine prefixes, installs winetricks verbs into them, and stores per-app launch settings.
requirements: Wine or Wine-staging installed via Homebrew or your package manager
DXVK or similar if you want Direct3D translation
patience for per-application debugging that is not in the code
whatYouLose: Per-application compatibility patches and known-good bottle recipes maintained by people who do this full time
A working answer for macOS oddities: Rosetta, 32-bit code, Apple's Game Porting Toolkit integration
Support you can actually email when a specific app breaks after an OS update
Graphics and audio plumbing that is already tuned instead of guessed
Funding the upstream Wine work that your DIY version is quietly standing on
moatNotes: The code is largely open. The compatibility database and the patch backlog are not.
whyPeopleStillPay: Because the failure mode of DIY Wine is not a missing feature, it is four hours of forum archaeology to learn that one app needs a specific DLL override and an older prefix architecture. CrossOver is a subscription to someone else having already done that for your exact app, plus a phone number when a macOS point release breaks everything. People who only need one or two Windows apps to work, and who bill their time at anything, tend to conclude that is a fine trade.
notes: The GUI is a weekend; the compatibility is not. The moat is a per-application patch and recipe database built over twenty-plus years, not the Wine source everyone can already download.
prompt:
Build a local desktop app called "Bottler": a GUI manager for Wine prefixes on macOS or Linux.

Stack, no alternatives:
- Tauri v2 with a React + TypeScript + Vite frontend, Rust backend.
- Tailwind for styling. No component library.
- Config stored as JSON at ~/.bottler/config.json. No database, no server, no accounts, no telemetry.

Assume wine, wineserver and winetricks are already on PATH. On startup, detect them and show a clear setup screen with install hints if missing. Do not try to install Wine yourself.

Core features:
1. Bottle list: each bottle is a Wine prefix directory under ~/.bottler/bottles/NAME, with metadata (display name, arch win32 or win64, wine binary path, notes, created date).
2. Create bottle: form for name and arch, then run WINEPREFIX=... WINEARCH=... wineboot -i and stream stdout/stderr into a live log pane.
3. Install into bottle: file picker for a .exe or .msi, run it under the selected prefix, stream the log.
4. Winetricks panel: a hardcoded list of about 20 common verbs (corefonts, vcrun2019, dotnet48, dxvk, d3dcompiler_47, etc). Clicking one runs winetricks against that prefix and streams output.
5. Shortcuts: per bottle, save named launch entries pointing at an .exe inside the prefix, with optional env var overrides (WINEDLLOVERRIDES, DXVK_HUD) and command line args. One click to launch.
6. Per bottle actions: open prefix folder in the file manager, run winecfg, kill wineserver, delete bottle with a typed confirmation.
7. Log pane with copy-to-clipboard and a persisted last-run log per bottle.

Explicitly out of scope: any curated compatibility database, automatic per-app fixes, game store integration, anti-cheat support, downloading installers, or claiming an app will work. Where relevant, show a plain disclaimer that compatibility is on the user.

Secrets: none needed. If you add any config for paths, read it from .env with a committed .env.example.

Deliver a README with exact dev and build commands, and make the app run with a single command after install.
